G4A01: A notch filter cuts a narrow slot to remove a steady carrier (a whistle) from the receiver passband.
G4A02: Switching CW to the other sideband moves interfering signals to the other side of your filter, so you may lose them.
G4A03: A noise blanker turns the receiver gain down for the instant of each noise pulse.
G4A04: Tune the plate for a pronounced dip in plate current: that is resonance.
G4A05: ALC holds back the drive so the amplifier isn't overdriven.
G4A06: A tuner matches the transmitter to the feed line, increasing the power transferred. It does not lower the SWR on the feed line itself.
G4A07: Too much noise reduction starts to distort the signals you want.
G4A08: Adjust LOAD for the power you want without exceeding the maximum plate current.
G4A09: The delay gives the amplifier's relay time to switch the antenna before RF arrives.
G4A10: An electronic keyer makes the dots and dashes automatically from paddle presses.
G4A11: ALC action distorts AFSK data signals, so set the audio so ALC stays inactive.
G4A12: Dual VFOs let you transmit on one frequency and listen on another (working split).
G4A13: An attenuator cuts very strong signals before they overload the receiver.
G4B01: Horizontal and vertical amplifiers move the trace on an oscilloscope.
G4B02: A scope shows the whole waveform, so it can measure complex waveforms a voltmeter can't.
G4B03: To see the keying waveform (its rise and fall), use an oscilloscope.
G4B04: Feed the attenuated RF output of the transmitter to the scope's vertical input to see the envelope.
G4B05: High input impedance draws almost no current, so the meter barely loads the circuit it measures.
G4B06: A digital multimeter reads with higher precision than an analog meter.
G4B07: A two-tone test uses two audio tones that are not harmonically related.
G4B08: A two-tone test checks linearity: how cleanly the transmitter amplifies.
G4B09: A moving needle is easier to watch when you're tuning for a peak or a dip.
G4B10: A directional wattmeter reads forward and reflected power, which gives you the SWR.
G4B11: An antenna analyzer measures SWR of the antenna and feed line connected to it. No transmitter needed.
G4B12: Strong nearby signals put received power into the analyzer and spoil its SWR readings.
G4B13: An antenna analyzer can measure the impedance of coax.
G4C01: A bypass capacitor shunts RF to ground while letting audio through.
G4C02: Arcing at a poor connection makes noise across a wide range of frequencies.
G4C03: SSB interference to audio gear sounds like distorted speech.
G4C04: CW interference to audio gear sounds like on-and-off humming or clicking, keyed with your sending.
G4C05: A ground wire can have high impedance at your frequency (for example, near a quarter wavelength long), so RF voltage builds up at the station end.
G4C06: A resonant ground wire puts high RF voltage on your equipment cases.
G4C07: A lightning strike's heat would melt a soldered joint. Use mechanical or welded connections.
G4C08: A ferrite choke on the cable blocks common-mode RF on its outside.
G4C09: Bond all enclosures together so there's no voltage difference to drive a loop current.
G4C10: A ground loop in audio wiring shows up as hum on your transmitted signal.
G4C11: Bonding all enclosures together keeps them at the same RF potential, so no hot spots.
G4C12: Grounding the chassis makes sure a fault can't leave dangerous voltage on the metal case.
G4D01: A speech processor makes your voice sound louder (more punch) without raising peak power.
G4D02: It raises the average power. Peak power stays the same.
G4D03: A badly set processor gives distortion, splatter (intermod) and lots of background noise. All of these.
G4D04: An S meter shows received signal strength.
G4D06: One S unit is about 6 dB.
G4D07: S8 to S9 is one S unit, 6 dB, about 4 times the power (3 dB = 2x, so 6 dB = 2 x 2).
G4D08: LSB lies below the displayed carrier: 7.178 - 0.003 = 7.175, so 7.175 to 7.178 MHz.
G4D09: USB lies above the displayed carrier: 14.347 + 0.003 = 14.350, so 14.347 to 14.350 MHz.
G4D10: LSB extends 3 kHz below the dial, so stay at least 3 kHz above the lower edge.
G4D11: USB extends 3 kHz above the dial, so stay at least 3 kHz below the upper edge.
G4E01: A capacitance hat adds capacitance at the top, making a short antenna act electrically longer.
G4E02: A corona ball rounds the tip so high RF voltage doesn't discharge into the air.
G4E03: Wire a 100 watt mobile straight to the battery with heavy wire (fused).
G4E04: A cigarette lighter socket's wiring is too light for the current a 100 watt rig draws.
G4E05: The biggest limit on HF mobile is the poor efficiency of the electrically short antenna.
G4E06: Shortened antennas have high Q, so their usable bandwidth is very narrow.
G4E07: Charging system, fuel system and control computers can all make noise in a car. All of these.
G4E08: Solar cells are wired series-parallel: series for voltage, parallel for current.
G4E09: A silicon solar cell gives about 0.5 volts open circuit.
G4E10: The series diode stops the battery from discharging back through the panel at night.
G4E11: A lithium iron phosphate battery needs a charge controller between it and the panel.
